title: Stone Game IX
statement:
Alice and Bob play with the stones in `stones`, where `stones[i]` is the value of stone `i`. They move alternately, Alice first, and each move takes away one remaining stone of the mover's choice.

- If, right after a move, the combined value of every stone taken so far (by either player) is a multiple of 3, the player who just moved loses at once.
- If all stones have been taken and nobody has lost that way, Bob is the winner, no matter whose turn it would be.

Both players play perfectly. Return `true` when Alice wins and `false` when Bob wins.
notes:
## Intuition

Only each stone's remainder mod 3 matters. A stone with remainder 0 never changes the running total mod 3, so taking it simply hands the turn to the other player. Among the other stones the order is forced: when the total is 1 mod 3 a 2 would hit a multiple of 3, so the mover needs a 1 (or a 0); when it is 2 mod 3 the mover needs a 2. Starting with a 1 the remainders must run 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, ...; starting with a 2 they run 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, ... The player whose needed remainder has run out (with no 0 to spare) loses, and if the stones run out first, Bob wins.

Zeros cancel in pairs (each one can be answered by another), so only whether their count is even matters. A brute force can try every move order with memoised minimax, but the counts alone decide the game.

## Approach

1. Count the stones by remainder into `count[0]`, `count[1]`, `count[2]`.
2. If `count[0]` is even, Alice opens with the rarer of 1 and 2; Bob is then the one who runs out first. That works exactly when both `count[1]` and `count[2]` are positive.
3. If `count[0]` is odd, the extra zero swaps the roles, so Alice must open with the more common remainder and needs it to exceed the other by more than 2; otherwise she gets stuck or the stones run out.

## Example 1, step by step

`stones = [2, 1]` gives `count = [0, 1, 1]`. `count[0] = 0` is even and both `count[1]` and `count[2]` are 1, so the answer is `true`: Alice takes either stone and Bob must take the other, making the total 3.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass to count remainders.
- Space: O(1): three counters.

## Pitfalls

- Running out of stones is a win for Bob, so Alice must force Bob onto a multiple of 3, not just survive.
- Remainder-0 stones are not irrelevant: their parity flips the result.
- In the odd case the gap must be greater than 2; a gap of exactly 2 still loses for Alice.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `count` | how many stones have remainder 0, 1 and 2 mod 3 |
| `stone` | the value of the stone being counted |

narration.2: Prepare one counter for each remainder mod 3.
narration.4: Only the remainder matters, so bump the counter for this stone's remainder.
narration.6: With an even number of zeros, the zeros cancel each other out.
narration.7: Alice wins exactly when she can open with one remainder and the other remainder exists to trap Bob.
narration.9: With an odd number of zeros the roles swap, so Alice needs one remainder to outnumber the other by more than 2.
